A beautiful definition of law in the young Hegel:
Law is a fragment of human nature.
Before the law, the criminal is nothing but the criminal. But law itself is only a fragment of human nature, and it therefore reaches only fragments of the human being.
There is historical proof—more than proof, in fact.
There is a fully valid and, both in form and substance, definitive model showing that there is no escape from the alternative:
homo homini deus—man is a god to man,
homo homini lupus—man is a wolf to man. And that also proves that we cannot remain at the neutral zero point of
homo homini homo—man is simply man to man.
The proof is the fate of the Roman Caesars.

From Hadrian onward—and according to Mommsen even earlier—the Roman Senate faced an unavoidable choice whenever a Caesar died: either declare the dead Caesar a god, or declare him an enemy, a princeps hostis.
The moment man tries to rise above himself—and he has to, because l’homme surpasse l’homme, man surpasses man—this alternative appears and the abyss opens.
